title: Following the Stars with Rubin
caption: Star trails above Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Cerro Pachón
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site
credit: NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/H. Stockebrand

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Circular star trails spin above Cerro Pachón in northern Chile, home of the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. The very long exposure records the apparent motion of the stars, along with other moving things such as aircraft and satellites, and the trails hint at the range of colors and brightnesses among the stars. At the center of the circles lies the southern celestial pole, in the dim constellation Octans, the Octant.

Studying the properties of stars with observatories like Rubin helps scientists learn how stars evolve. Across the 10-year survey known as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), Rubin is expected to measure about 17 billion stars.

When Rubin spots a star changing in brightness, it will issue an alert within minutes. Astronomers can then follow short- and long-term changes that are hard to track without a continuous survey. These include flickers or pulses ahead of supernovae, new variable stars whose brightness shifts over several years, and rare events such as mergers of dense neutron stars.

understand.summary: An extra-long-exposure night photograph by Hernán Stockebrand. No camera or exposure details or color mapping are published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points, and the trails appear only because the camera kept recording while Earth turned.
